results.title: Counterexample to the first Zassenhaus conjecture (Kourovka 17.67)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There exist a finite group $G$ and a unit $u$ of finite order of the integral group ring $\mathbb{Z}G$ such that for every unit $v$ of the rational group ring $\mathbb{Q}G$, every $g \in G$ and every sign $\varepsilon \in \{1, -1\}$, the conjugate $v u v^{-1}$, computed in $\mathbb{Q}G$, is not equal to $\varepsilon g$. That is, the first Zassenhaus conjecture is false.

results.title: Morita's p-adic gamma values at natural numbers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a prime $p$ and a natural number $n$, this is the $p$-adic integer $(-1)^n \prod_{0 < j < n,\ p \nmid j} j$: $(-1)^n$ times the product of the positive integers below $n$ that are not divisible by $p$. results.title: Monotone 3-SAT instances
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A monotone 3-SAT instance is a pair $(n, \varphi)$ of a natural number $n$, the number of variables, and a CNF formula $\varphi$.

results.title: Well-formed monotone 3-SAT instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A monotone 3-SAT instance $(n, \varphi)$ is well formed when every clause of the CNF formula $\varphi$ is a list of exactly three literals (repetitions allowed), each with a variable below $n$, and the literals of each clause are all positive or all negative.

results.title: Satisfiable monotone 3-SAT instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A monotone 3-SAT instance $(n, \varphi)$ is feasible when there is a list of $n$ truth values $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ such that the assignment sending each variable $x < n$ to $a_x$ and every variable $x \ge n$ to false satisfies the CNF formula $\varphi$.

results.title: MONOTONE 3-SAT as a decision problem

results.title: MONOTONE 3-SAT is NP-complete
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The decision problem MONOTONE 3-SAT belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to MONOTONE 3-SAT.

results.title: Public-coin randomized protocol
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A family `run r` of deterministic protocols indexed by the shared random string `r : R`; the string is drawn uniformly from the finite set `R`, independently of the inputs (A. Rao and A. Yehudayoff, *Communication Complexity*, early draft, Chapter 3).

results.title: Cost of a public-coin protocol
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The largest depth of the deterministic protocols it runs, over all random strings.

results.title: Error probability of a public-coin protocol
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For `f : X → Y → Bool` and an input pair `(x, y)`, the fraction of random strings `r : R` on which `run r` outputs a value other than `f x y`.

results.title: Each run costs at most the cost
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every deterministic protocol run by a public-coin protocol has depth at most its cost.

results.title: Collision count of a uniformly random function
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For distinct points `a ≠ b` of a finite type, exactly a `1 / |β|` fraction of the functions `h : α → β` satisfy `h a = h b`: `|{h | h a = h b}| · |β| = |α → β|`.

results.title: Random-hash protocol for equality
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: With shared random function `h : {0,1}^n → {0,1}^k`, Alice sends the `k` bits of `h x` and Bob announces whether they equal `h y` (A. Rao and A. Yehudayoff, *Communication Complexity*, early draft, Chapter 3, Figure 3.1).

results.title: Output of the random-hash protocol
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: With shared random function `h`, the protocol outputs `true` exactly when `h x = h y`.

results.title: Cost of the random-hash protocol
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The random-hash protocol for equality costs at most `k + 1` bits.

results.title: No error on equal inputs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The random-hash protocol never errs when `x = y`.

results.title: Error of the random-hash protocol for equality
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: On distinct inputs the random-hash protocol errs with probability exactly `1 / 2 ^ k`: it errs exactly when the random function collides on `x` and `y` (A. Rao and A. Yehudayoff, *Communication Complexity*, early draft, Chapter 3: "if `x ≠ y`, the probability that `h(x) = h(y)` is at most `2^-k`").

results.title: Randomized protocol
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A finitely supported probability distribution on deterministic protocols: the protocol actually run is drawn from it, independently of the inputs, and both parties see the draw (A. Rao and A. Yehudayoff, *Communication Complexity*, early draft, Chapter 3: "a randomized protocol can be thought of as a distribution on deterministic protocols").

results.title: Cost of a randomized protocol
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The largest depth of a deterministic protocol in its support.

results.title: Error of a randomized protocol
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The probability that the drawn protocol answers wrongly for `f` on the input pair `(x, y)`.

results.title: A public-coin protocol as a randomized protocol
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The uniform distribution on the random strings, pushed forward along `run`.

results.title: The two notions of error agree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The error of a public-coin protocol, as a fraction of random strings, is the error of the randomized protocol it defines.

results.title: Cost of the induced randomized protocol
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: It is at most the cost of the public-coin protocol.

results.title: Randomized communication complexity
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: `randComplexity f ε` is the least cost of a randomized protocol whose error on every input pair is at most `ε` (A. Rao and A. Yehudayoff, *Communication Complexity*, early draft, Chapter 3, "worst-case" error). For finite inputs and `ε ≥ 0` such a protocol exists. If none meets the bound (for instance when `ε < 0`, or possibly for infinite inputs), the value is `0` by the convention `sInf ∅ = 0`.

results.title: Randomized communication complexity of equality
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every `n` and `k`, equality of `n`-bit strings has randomized communication complexity at most `k + 1` with error `2 ^ (-k)`, by the random-hash protocol (A. Rao and A. Yehudayoff, *Communication Complexity*, early draft, Chapter 3, Figure 3.1); deterministically it needs `n + 1` bits for `n ≥ 1` (`commComplexity_eqFn`).

results.title: Error indicator of a protocol
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: `1` if the protocol `p` answers wrongly on `(x, y)` for the function `f`, and `0` if it answers correctly.

results.title: Distributional error of a deterministic protocol
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a distribution `μ` on input pairs, the probability under `μ` that `p` answers wrongly for `f`.

results.title: Distributional communication complexity
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: `distComplexity f μ ε` is the least depth of a deterministic protocol whose error under the input distribution `μ` is at most `ε` (A. Rao and A. Yehudayoff, *Communication Complexity*, early draft, Chapter 3, "average-case" error; fixing the random string, a randomized protocol does no better against a fixed distribution). For `ε ≥ 0` such a protocol exists; otherwise the value is `0` by the convention `sInf ∅ = 0`.

results.title: Distributional complexity is at most randomized complexity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Against any input distribution `μ`, some deterministic protocol in the support of an optimal randomized protocol has `μ`-error at most `ε` (the easy direction of A. Rao and A. Yehudayoff, *Communication Complexity*, early draft, Theorem 3.3).

results.title: Yao's minimax principle for communication complexity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For finite input sets and `ε ≥ 0`, the randomized communication complexity of `f` with error at most `ε` on every input equals the largest, over distributions `μ` on input pairs, of the least depth of a deterministic protocol with error at most `ε` under `μ` (A. Rao and A. Yehudayoff, *Communication Complexity*, early draft, Theorem 3.3, proved there from von Neumann's minimax theorem).

results.title: Error probability of a private-coin protocol
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a deterministic protocol `p` in which Alice holds `(x, a)` and Bob holds `(y, b)`, the fraction of pairs `(a, b) ∈ RA × RB` of private random strings on which `p` outputs a value other than `f x y`.

results.title: Set intersection function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: `disjFn n x y` is `true` iff the subsets of `{1, …, n}` with characteristic vectors `x` and `y` intersect; this is the function `DISₙ` of N. Alon, Y. Matias and M. Szegedy, J. Comput. System Sci. 58 (1999), Section 3 (its negation is set disjointness).

results.title: Randomized communication complexity of disjointness
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every fixed $0 \le \varepsilon < 1/2$ there is $c > 0$ such that, for every $n$, every public-coin protocol that decides whether two subsets of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ intersect, with error at most $\varepsilon$ on every input, has worst-case cost at least $cn$: $R_\varepsilon(\mathrm{DIS}_n) \ge cn$.
